title: Overdose with bradycardia + hypotension + wheezing + hypoglycemia = beta blocker
vignette: A 30-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after an intentional overdose of one of his own medications. He is lethargic and minimally responsive. Blood pressure is 76/46 mm Hg and pulse is 38/min. Auscultation reveals diffuse wheezing. Fingerstick glucose is 48 mg/dL (normal 70-100). An ECG shows sinus bradycardia without QRS widening. Which of the following medications did this patient most likely ingest?

clues.text: intentional overdose of one of his own medications
clues.note: An intentional medication overdose frames this as a toxicology identification: match the vital-sign and metabolic pattern to a drug class. (Sensitive presentation - handled as clinical toxicology.)

clues.text: Blood pressure is 76/46 mm Hg and pulse is 38/min
clues.note: Simultaneous severe hypotension (76/46) and bradycardia (38 / normal 60-100) indicate a cardiovascular depressant - classically a beta blocker or a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker.
Bronchospasm/wheezing points specifically to a (non-selective) BETA BLOCKER - beta-2 blockade in the airways - and away from calcium channel blockers, which do not cause bronchospasm.
Hypoglycemia (48 / normal 70-100) favors beta blocker toxicity (blunted glycogenolysis/gluconeogenesis), whereas calcium channel blocker overdose classically causes HYPERglycemia.

whatMatters: Bradycardia + hypotension + bronchospasm (wheezing) + HYPOglycemia is the fingerprint of BETA BLOCKER overdose. Beta-1 blockade slows the heart and drops blood pressure, beta-2 blockade causes bronchospasm, and loss of beta-adrenergic glycogenolysis lowers glucose. Answer A. (A non-DHP calcium channel blocker gives bradycardia/hypotension too, but with HYPERglycemia and no wheeze.)
strategy: Use the discriminators. Both beta blockers and non-DHP calcium channel blockers cause bradycardia + hypotension, so look at the extras: wheezing + hypoglycemia = beta blocker; hyperglycemia (impaired insulin release) = calcium channel blocker. Digoxin causes GI/visual symptoms and arrhythmias with hyperkalemia; opioids cause respiratory depression/miosis; benzodiazepines cause sedation without this hemodynamic collapse.

eliminations.label: Non-DHP calcium channel blocker - hyperglycemia, no wheeze
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: verapamil/diltiazem overdose, which also causes bradycardia and hypotension. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: calcium channel blocker toxicity classically produces HYPERglycemia (blocked pancreatic insulin release) and does NOT cause bronchospasm - opposite of this patient's hypoglycemia and wheezing. ✅ Correct if: bradycardia/hypotension WITH hyperglycemia.

eliminations.label: Digoxin - GI/visual + hyperkalemia pattern
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: digoxin toxicity causes nausea/vomiting, visual changes (yellow halos), and various arrhythmias. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it presents with hyperkalemia and characteristic ECG/arrhythmias, not bronchospasm and hypoglycemia. ✅ Correct if: nausea + yellow vision + hyperkalemia + arrhythmia.

eliminations.label: Opioid - respiratory depression + miosis
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: opioid overdose causes CNS/respiratory depression with pinpoint pupils. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: the hallmark is hypoventilation and miosis, not bradycardia with bronchospasm and hypoglycemia. ✅ Correct if: depressed respirations + pinpoint pupils (reverse with naloxone).

eliminations.label: Benzodiazepine - sedation without hemodynamic collapse
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: benzodiazepine overdose causes sedation and mild respiratory depression. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it does not typically produce profound bradycardia/hypotension, wheezing, or hypoglycemia. ✅ Correct if: isolated sedation with stable vitals (reverse cautiously with flumazenil).

reasoning: Overdose with severe bradycardia + hypotension = cardiovascular depressant (beta blocker vs non-DHP CCB)
Wheezing (bronchospasm) + hypoglycemia are specific to beta blockade
Non-DHP CCB would instead cause hyperglycemia and no bronchospasm
mechanism: Beta blockers antagonize catecholamines at beta-adrenergic receptors. Beta-1 blockade in the heart reduces heart rate (bradycardia) and contractility, lowering cardiac output and blood pressure; in overdose this produces profound bradycardia and hypotension. Beta-2 blockade (with non-selective agents such as propranolol) causes bronchoconstriction, hence the wheezing. Beta-adrenergic signaling also normally promotes hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis and masks adrenergic warning signs of low glucose; blocking it can cause hypoglycemia. Together, bradycardia + hypotension + bronchospasm + hypoglycemia is a classic beta blocker overdose pattern. The key mimic, a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker (verapamil/diltiazem), shares the bradycardia/hypotension but causes HYPERglycemia (calcium channel blockade impairs pancreatic insulin secretion) and no bronchospasm. Beta blocker toxicity is treated with IV fluids, atropine, glucagon (which raises cardiac cAMP bypassing the beta receptor), and high-dose insulin-euglycemia therapy.

difficulty.label: 📚 Pure knowledge gap
difficulty.message: First Aid Pharm/Tox > beta blocker overdose: bradycardia, hypotension, bronchospasm, hypoglycemia; antidote glucagon; contrast CCB overdose (hyperglycemia).

difficulty.label: 🧭 Understanding the question
difficulty.message: Two toxins cause bradycardia + hypotension; the wheeze + low glucose select the beta blocker.

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocabulary
difficulty.message: Unsure on beta-1 vs beta-2 effects, glycogenolysis, non-DHP CCB, or glucagon antidote? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🧲 Pulled by a distractor
difficulty.message: Non-DHP CCB (hyperglycemia, no wheeze), digoxin (GI/visual/hyperkalemia), opioid (miosis/respiratory depression), benzodiazepine (sedation) don't fit the full tetrad.

difficulty.label: ✍️ Something else
difficulty.message: Bank: beta blocker OD -> bradycardia + hypotension + bronchospasm + hypoglycemia; glucagon antidote. CCB OD -> hyperglycemia.

keywords.back: Glucagon (raises cardiac cAMP, bypassing beta receptor)
Blocked glycogenolysis/gluconeogenesis + masked adrenergic warning signs
Bronchospasm (avoid nonselective beta blockers in asthma)

firstAid.detail: Pharm: bradycardia, hypotension, bronchospasm, hypoglycemia; treat with glucagon.

firstAid.detail: Pharm > glucagon (beta blocker), calcium/insulin (CCB), naloxone (opioid), flumazenil (benzodiazepine).

memoryHook: Beta blocker overdose hits all four betas at once: slow heart, low pressure, tight airways, low sugar - and glucagon is the escape hatch.
